name: tipping.elements
summary: The climate tipping elements from data/events/tipping.toml, each with the global warming at which an assessment judged it likely to tip (a central estimate and a range) and its timescale, checked every year against the run's global anomaly. A tipping.crossing event the first year the run passes an element's low end and again its central estimate. The table is the claim; the module only compares. With coupling above zero the file's coupling rows act: once an element has passed its threshold, the elements it is coupled to have their thresholds lowered by the row's fraction times the strength, so one crossing can bring the next within reach in the same run (Wunderling et al. 2021: interacting elements lower each other's critical temperatures, the ice sheets start cascades, the Atlantic circulation carries them).

name: policy.capacity
summary: Derailment: the world's capacity to cut emissions, 0 to 1, eroded by what the run's own warming does to people and recovering slowly, after Dyke (The Conversation, 2026-11-05): the consequences of climate change erode the capacity to address its causes, through debt, conflict and backlash, and collective action is easier to destroy than to build. Each January the capacity moves toward a target set by the share of people under heat stress (from the regions module), amplified where the people-weighted fairness band is low; it falls fast and recovers slowly, the recovery scaled by the voice band; a wild card knocks it by its kind for some years; and where a country's people are under stress a conflict may be drawn, which takes a fraction of that country's people and knocks the capacity by the country's share of the world. name: quake.ground
summary: This module supplies the ground motion for a scenario earthquake. It does not simulate the fault or the shaking. It reads published maps from an event folder: the peak acceleration and velocity of the ground at the surface, and the probability and extent of liquefaction and landslides, for saturated or dry soil. A file in the folder, ground.toml, names the maps and their source. At the moment set for the earthquake, the module makes the maps available to the other modules and announces the rupture. name: quake.buildings
summary: This module estimates building damage, deaths, injuries and displaced people in each cell of the map, from the ground module's shaking. For each cell it uses a fragility curve, which gives the probability that a building reaches each of four damage states at a given peak ground acceleration. One set of curves stands for a generic mix of building types. The module adds the buildings lost where the ground liquefies or slides, then applies a casualty rate to each damage state. This is the approach of Hazus, the loss-estimation software of the Federal Emergency Management Agency. The buildings, the residents and the occupants by time of day are maps in the event folder. The default values of the curves and of the casualty rates are recalled from memory and have not been checked against the Hazus manual. A scenario may adjust the scales below to fit a published loss study, and a run that carries an obs.losses module reports how close the result is to that study. In this model only shaking makes a building collapse, and nearly all deaths are in collapsed buildings. The toll therefore changes less between day and night, and between saturated and dry soil, than a Hazus run's does.

name: portland.lifelines
summary: This module is specific to Portland. It follows the city after the earthquake one day at a time. It tracks the twelve bridges over the Willamette River, thirteen hospitals and their backup generators, electricity, water, and the fuel stored at the Critical Energy Infrastructure Hub, the strip of fuel terminals in northwest Portland. It keeps an account of the hub's fuel in gallons, which must balance every day. The module has two modes. In the computed mode other modules do the work: fuel.tanks the spill, roads.bridges each bridge, roads.routes the open roads, power.structures the electricity service, health.hospitals the hospitals and fuel.depot the fuel account. This module then only restores water on its schedule, tells the story of the bridges, roads and services, and gathers the day's state for the modules that count harm to people. In the ranges mode it draws those outcomes at random from published ranges: Multnomah County's statement on its bridges, the Oregon Resilience Plan's restoration times and the county's 2022 study of the hub's tanks. Water service follows the Resilience Plan's range in both modes. Three inputs are guesses in both modes: how much generator fuel a hospital holds, how much fuel the emergency response uses each day, and the day fuel deliveries resume. This run uses the ranges mode.

views.title: what this module leaves out
views.source: The model has no tsunami (none is expected to reach Portland), no aftershocks and no fire following the earthquake. It leaves out the Columbia River bridges and Interstate 5 to the north, sewage, telephone and data networks, food supply, the airport, the port, and people leaving the city. Water pipes are not modelled. The Portland Water Bureau's estimate of 1,500 to 3,000 pipe breaks reached this project only through a search summary and is not used. Water service returns along a straight line to a day drawn from a published range, and so does electricity in the ranges mode, whereas a real recovery is uneven from one neighbourhood to the next. Whether a hospital is damaged depends on a generic building fragility curve at its location and a guessed allowance for newer building codes. The fuel at the hub is a single stock, with no pipes, no individual trucks and no priorities among users. The spill is a quantity, either drawn from the range in the county's study or summed over the failed tanks. The model does not follow the fuel once it reaches the river.

name: people.aftermath
summary: This module counts harm to people in the days and months after an earthquake. It does not model how that harm comes about. It applies a short table of rates, each with a source, to counts the run already has: the life-threatening injuries from the shaking, the days people spend without electricity or water, and the people who depend on electrically powered medical devices. name: fuel.tanks
summary: This module damages storage tanks one at a time. Each tank sits at its own coordinates. At the earthquake it reads the ground motion there and is assigned a damage state by a random draw against a fragility curve, which gives the probability of each state at a given strength of shaking and of ground failure. A tank at or beyond the curve's failing state releases a share of its contents. The share depends on the tank's age: a tank built before the design year in the folder's rule, or with no recorded year, draws its share from the range in its own row of the table, and a newer tank releases at most the rule's smaller maximum. The release goes toward water where the tank's row says so. The tanks are the event folder's tanks.csv, and the curve and the age rule are its fragility.toml. The module does not follow the fuel after it leaves the tank, and it has no fire.

Each change is published, so a module that routes traffic or draws a map can follow it. The bridges are the event folder's bridges.toml, and the curves and repair times are its fragility.toml, which says where each came from.

name: power.structures
summary: This module computes electricity service from the transmission structures that are standing. Each structure, a tower or a pole, is a row in a table in the event folder, with a location and a probability of failure for saturated and for dry soil. At the earthquake each structure fails or stands by a random draw against its probability. The modelled area is divided into coarse cells, and a cell has electricity when the structures nearest to it are all standing. Afterwards crews repair a fixed number of structures a day, starting with those that serve the most people. Each day the module writes a map of where electricity is on, which other modules read at the places they care about, and reports the share of residents served. The structures are not connected into a network: the module has no power lines, substations, generation or neighbourhood distribution, so none of those can fail in it and it restores service sooner than a real grid would.

name: roads.routes
summary: This module holds a road network as segments joined in a graph and works out what can be reached over it. Each segment has a class of expected ground deformation. At the earthquake a segment with a class above zero closes for a number of days drawn at random from the range for its class, and it reopens when those days have passed. A bridge joins one segment on each bank; it is open or closed as the bridges module reports. Each day the module finds which named places can be reached from one origin over open segments and open bridges, and reports the share of the network's length that is open. The graph and the named places are the event folder's routes.toml, and the closure ranges are its fragility.toml. Debris from damaged buildings does not block a segment, and the module has no traffic, no detours off the listed segments and no vehicles.

name: fuel.depot
summary: This module keeps the account of one fuel depot, in gallons, in a ledger that must balance at every close. The depot starts with the contents the event folder gives it, less any cut made before the earthquake. When the tanks module reports what the tanks released, that fuel leaves the stock for the ground and for the water. Each day afterwards the emergency response draws a fixed amount, but only once the roads module reports that a truck can get from the depot to at least one place. Any module may ask for a delivery, and the depot grants it while it has the fuel. From a stated day, resupply tops the stock back up toward what it held. The module also carries a published range for deaths and injuries at the depot itself, where the folder gives one: it draws a value in the range at random and scales it by the size of the release. It does not model fire, and it does not follow the spilled fuel.

summary: This module says where the water is. It reads ESA WorldCover 2021, a land-cover map made from satellite images at 10 metres, and marks each cell of the run's grid that is mostly permanent open water: rivers, lakes and harbours. Other modules can read that map. When the tanks module reports a release that goes toward water, this module sets the gallons down on the water cell nearest the tank, so the map shows where the spill meets the river. It does not model water: there is no flow, no river level, no tide and no movement of anything on the surface, so the fuel stays where it arrives. A release with no water within reach is counted as stranded.

name: health.hospitals
summary: This module follows hospitals and whether each one has power. At the earthquake each hospital building is damaged or not by a random draw against a generic building fragility curve at the ground motion at its location, with an allowance for hospitals being built to a newer code. An undamaged hospital is open while the grid reaches it, which the module learns by reading the power module's map of service at the hospital. When the grid does not reach it, the hospital runs on its generator and uses up its stored fuel. If the roads module reports that a truck can reach it, it asks the fuel depot for a day's delivery, and a granted delivery refills the generator. A hospital whose generator fuel runs out is without power until the grid or a delivery returns. The module does not represent beds, staff, supplies or damage inside a building that still stands, so an open hospital here is a building with power and nothing more.

name: people.agents
summary: This module represents the residents as agents, each standing for a fixed number of people set by the scale parameter. It creates them at the start of the run from the event folder's maps of where people are. Each agent gets a home cell, drawn in proportion to residents, and a work cell, drawn in proportion to daytime occupants. A share of the agents depend on electrically powered medical devices; the share comes from counts in the event folder's aftermath.toml. At the earthquake each agent is at work by day or at home by night. It is placed in a collapsed or a standing building according to the share of buildings that collapsed in that cell, and it dies or is displaced at the rates the buildings module gives for the cell. The agents' death count should agree with the buildings module's count by cell. In the daytime runs of the Portland scenario made on 12 November 2026 it is lower, for a reason not yet found. On each day afterwards an agent has electricity or not according to its home cell, and water according to the schedule for the whole area. The agents make no decisions yet. They are here so that a later version can let them leave, seek shelter or travel, and the module reports how fast it runs so that the cost of that is known.

name: obs.losses
summary: This module holds a run's building damage and casualties against a published loss study. It computes nothing about the earthquake. Once the buildings module has finished, it sums that module's results for each cell over the small areas the study reports by and over one named group of larger areas, and reports how the two sets of numbers compare: a ratio for the group's deaths, displaced people, injuries and damaged buildings, and a correlation across the small areas. A file in the event folder, losses.toml, names the study, its tables and its columns. A ratio near 1 does not make the run an independent estimate if the buildings module's parameters were fitted to the same study, and the buildings module says where they were.
